title: /wayfinder: Nothing is too big to plan anymore

note.argument: The speaker begins by noting that existing AI planning tools are limited to a single session, which forces users to break large projects into tiny chunks and curtails ambition. To overcome this, they present Wayfinder, a skill that maps a project as a set of decision tickets (research, prototype, grilling, and tasks) and tracks the "fog of war" across multiple agent sessions. Wayfinder orchestrates parallel and dependent work, integrates with any coding agent and any issue‑tracker, and can even handle real‑world tasks. By generating non‑persistent specs and encouraging frequent prototyping, it avoids waterfall‑style upfront design while still providing a concrete destination. The speaker argues that for work that cannot be completed in one session, Wayfinder offers a systematic, scalable way to plan and execute, even for non‑coding endeavors.
claims: I have figured out a way to plan work of any size using an AI agent.
Existing planning tools are too constrained because they are tied to a single session.

Wayfinder can orchestrate planning of enormous chunks of work across multiple sessions.

title: Don't waste time on specs: /prototype instead

note.argument: The speaker begins by observing that many developers feel compelled to write exhaustive specifications before involving AI, mistakenly believing that a perfect spec guarantees correct output. He points out that this impulse ignores the fact that code can be written incrementally, using throwaway prototypes that directly answer design questions. Because the cost of generating code has dropped dramatically, creating quick, high‑fidelity prototypes is now cheap and highly effective. By integrating a dedicated "prototype" skill into his Wayfinder planning system, he can raise the fidelity of discussions when needed, turning abstract questions into concrete, testable artifacts. Although higher‑fidelity prototypes consume more tokens, they provide clearer answers than low‑fidelity conversation, reducing the gap between spec and production code. Consequently, he argues that teams should replace over‑specification with iterative prototyping—both for UI and back‑end logic—to achieve faster, more reliable outcomes.
claims: People think they need to create a detailed spec for AI before getting useful outputs.
You can actually write code while working towards a spec, using throwaway prototypes to answer questions.
A prototype is throwaway code that answers a question.
The cost of producing code has gone way, way down, making prototypes cheaper than ever and a more effective tool.
Producing prototypes (quick throwaway spikes) has never been cheaper and never been a more effective tool.

title: Learn anything with the /teach skill

note.argument: The speaker begins by reflecting on a decade of teaching experience and the desire to encapsulate that expertise in an AI skill. Observing that effective teaching requires tracking a learner's progress, they argue that the skill must be stateful rather than stateless, explaining the distinction between the two. They design the /teach skill to be stateful, incorporating components such as a mission file, curated high‑trust resources, concise HTML lessons, quizzes, and learning records, all guided by the zone of proximal development to keep learners optimally challenged. Demonstrating the skill with a Rubik's Cube tutorial, they show how it adapts to the learner's state and provides interactive feedback. The speaker then extrapolates the utility of such a skill to engineering contexts like onboarding, and positions developers as the first community to experience AI's strengths—particularly code generation—giving them a unique advantage to pioneer AI‑augmented learning tools.

title: 9 Things People Get Wrong With My /grill-* skills

note.argument: The author begins by defining Grill Me skills as a relentless questioning process that requires the user to be a good planner. He then warns that overly large scopes introduce hidden high‑fidelity questions and can exceed a model’s token limit, pushing it into a “dumb zone.” Effective use therefore demands active participation—neither passive surrender to endless low‑fidelity queries nor over‑active fixation on them. The author stresses preserving the context and design decisions made during grilling, rather than discarding them, and insists on using sufficiently capable models because grilling leans on their parametric knowledge. Finally, he proposes running two (or more) grilling sessions in parallel to increase planning throughput. Together, these points form a step‑by‑step guide to avoid common failure modes and get the most out of the Grill Me skills.

title: /handoff is my new favourite skill

note.argument: The author begins by noting that large language‑model agents suffer a performance drop as their context window fills, defining a "smart zone" (roughly the first 120 k tokens) and a "dumb zone" beyond that. Existing tools like compact can summarise a conversation to move it back into the smart zone, but compact either clobbers progress or creates a layered sediment of summaries that can become inefficient. To preserve the purity of a current session while still tackling out‑of‑scope tasks, the author created the handoff skill, which extracts the relevant slice of context, writes a concise markdown hand‑off document, and saves it to a temporary location. This enables parallel sessions, prototyping, and a DIY sub‑agent workflow where learnings are compressed and fed back to the original session. The author also codifies best practices for hand‑off documents—saving them temporarily, redacting sensitive data, avoiding duplication, and including a suggested‑skill section—to make the process reliable and portable across different agents. The conclusion is that handoff is an essential, reusable tool in the author’s workflow for managing context limits and orchestrating multi‑session development.

title: Burn through the backlog from hell with /triage

note.argument: The speaker begins by diagnosing a gap: most skill‑based automation works for solo developers but breaks down in team settings where many people contribute ideas and bug reports. To fill that gap they present a new skill, triage, which they have already deployed across all their open‑source repos. They explain that triage works by attaching a state‑machine of category and state labels to each issue, guaranteeing that every issue has exactly one of each. This labeling scheme lets the system automatically distinguish bugs from enhancements, and further classify them (needs triage, needs info, ready for agent, etc.). By requiring a brief before an issue can be marked “ready for agent,” the skill creates a clean hand‑off point for autonomous agents. The speaker demonstrates the workflow: the AI lists untriaged issues, applies labels, diagnoses bugs, writes fixes, and pushes changes, all while monitoring context usage. The argument concludes that this label‑driven pipeline turns noisy human input into well‑defined tasks that autonomous agents can reliably consume, and that the approach dovetails with other skills like PRD generation.

title: How To De-Slop A Codebase Ruined By AI (with one skill)

note.argument: The speaker begins by observing that AI has accelerated software entropy, causing codebases to degrade faster as incremental changes introduce hidden problems. To counter this, they advocate restructuring code into deep modules—units with simple interfaces that hide complex implementations—because deep modules provide locality for maintainers and leverage for users. They define the terminology (modules, interfaces, seams, adapters) and explain how deep modules improve testability and maintainability. Using an AI‑driven "improve code base architecture" skill, developers can identify shallow‑module hotspots and refactor them into deeper modules, but the AI only supplies suggestions; a human strategic programmer must evaluate and apply them. Regular use of the skill, combined with good testing harnesses, is recommended, especially for legacy (i.e., shallow‑module, bad) codebases.

title: Never Trust An LLM

note.argument: The speaker begins by observing that large language models frequently produce false statements—"hallucinations"—and that this unreliability has made him and many other developers distrust them. He categorises hallucinations (factual errors, fabricated entities, contextual inconsistencies) and distinguishes between intrinsic (information supplied in the current conversation) and extrinsic (knowledge the model must retrieve from its training data) sources. He then explains why hallucinations occur: the training process compresses vast amounts of data, discarding detail, so the model often has only a low‑resolution representation of facts and therefore guesses when asked about missing information. Moreover, benchmark‑driven evaluation rewards confident guesses over admissions of uncertainty, reinforcing this behavior. From this analysis he concludes that LLMs can be useful if used correctly—by feeding them the necessary context (intrinsic information) or by forcing them to fetch up‑to‑date data via a search tool—while still remaining skeptical of any extrinsic answers they generate.
claims: LLMs lie. They lie all the time.
Hallucinations are so unbelievably common that I am now paranoid about everything an LLM says to me and I will never ever trust an LLM.
Every software developer I talk to shares the same intuition that LLMs hallucinate constantly.
LLMs are unreliable, especially when you rely on their extrinsic knowledge.
LLMs are much more reliable when you provide them with the information first.

title: Claude Code tried to improve /init... Is it any better?

note.argument: The speaker begins by testing the newly released Claude code init command, noting that it asks the user a series of setup questions. Evaluating each suggested addition to Claude.md, he accepts a single line about useEffect reducer as a cheap safeguard, rejects redundant entries such as testing patterns and build commands that Claude can already infer, and dismisses an explanatory header that adds no value. He praises the new init script for producing a far smaller Claude.md and a useful skill (npm‑install‑force for effect packages) compared to the previous bloated version, while still urging the team to make the system less sycophantic and more proactive. The overall conclusion is that a minimal, non‑redundant Claude.md combined with targeted skills represents a genuine improvement, provided the UI and suggestion logic are refined.

title: Building a REAL feature with Claude Code: every step explained

note.argument: The speaker begins by rejecting the hype that Claude code represents a brand‑new paradigm, arguing instead that existing software‑development practices—incremental design, feedback loops, and treating tools as teammates—apply just as well. He identifies concrete pain points in his current system: the cumbersome two‑step ghost‑lesson workflow, the lack of a direct delete UI for real lessons, and the inability to create courses without a file‑system path. He proposes a set of concrete enhancements—direct creation of real lessons, a “ghost course” concept with a nullable file‑path column, UI changes to expose delete and creation actions, and a materialisation cascade that automatically creates on‑disk artifacts when needed. To flesh out these ideas he uses Claude to ask clarifying questions, capture a ubiquitous‑language glossary, and generate a concise PRD. The PRD is broken into bite‑sized GitHub issues, each with clear acceptance criteria. An autonomous “AFK” agent (Ralph) then iterates over the issues, writing code, tests, and commit messages while the author QA‑tests in parallel, feeding back bugs and refinements. The loop continues until the feature set is complete, demonstrating that the combination of human‑in‑the‑loop design, AI‑generated specifications, and autonomous implementation yields a rapid, reliable development process.
claims: The techniques we’ve been using for the past 20 years work really well with Claude code.
You get the most out of Claude code when you treat it like a teammate you would delegate work to.
Ghost courses let me plan courses without having to commit to a concrete file‑system path.
Once a course has a file‑system path it stays a real course forever because the on‑disk representation never disappears.
To support ghost courses the courses table’s file‑path column must be made nullable.
